steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on KnowDDI, a drug-drug interaction prediction method that learns knowledge subgraphs from a combined DDI network and external knowledge graph. Motivate why DDI prediction matters, cover prior graph learning and KG-based methods and their limits, and summarize our approach and results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why DDI prediction matters (combination therapies vs. adverse reactions)
- Computational DDI prediction and the data scarcity problem
- External biomedical knowledge graphs and existing KG-based methods
- Our method: KnowDDI
- Results and broader potential

  - over-parameterized deep models can't use expressive power, may be worse than two-stage embedding methods

  - agencies (National Center for Biotechnology Information, European Bioinformatics Institute) maintain public biomedical data resources
  - integrated into KGs: Hetionet, PharmKG, PrimeKG
  - rich prior knowledge, may compensate for lack of samples

  - later works: merge DDI network + KG, extract enclosing subgraphs per drug-pair, predict from concatenated drug node embeddings + subgraph embedding
  - problem: KGs built by automated process or experts -> noise/inconsistent info not filtered
  - leveraging external KGs still challenging
- KnowDDI
  - merge DDI graph + external KG into combined network; learn generic representations for all nodes
  - extract drug-flow subgraph per drug-pair
  - learn knowledge subgraph from generic representations + drug-flow subgraph
  - drug representations become more predictive of DDI types
  - knowledge subgraph has explaining paths: edges of important known DDIs or new edges linking highly similar drugs
  - filters irrelevant info, adds resembling relationships; lack of DDIs compensated by enriched representations + propagated similarities
- Results and potential
  - extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, consistently outperforms existing works
  - case studies: convincing explaining paths
  - potential: protein-protein, drug-target, disease-gene interactions; advancing biomedicine and healthcare

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Predicting drug-drug interaction (DDI) accurately is important in biomedicine and healthcare. One reason is combination therapies, where several drugs are used together, which can treat complex disease and comorbidities, for example human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). A recent study shows that combination therapies like lopinavir together with ritonavir may also treat coronavirus disease (COVID-19), which is the infectious disease that caused a global pandemic in the past three years. The other reason is that DDI is an important cause of adverse drug reactions. These account for 1% hospitalizations in the general population and 2-5% hospital admissions in the elderly. For example if warfarin and aspirin are taken together, they compete for binding to plasma proteins. The warfarin that cannot be bound to plasma proteins then remains in the blood, and this results in acute bleeding in patients.

Finding DDIs from clinical evidence such as laboratory studies is extremely costly and takes a lot of time. So in recent years computational techniques, especially deep learning, have been developed to speed up finding potential DDIs. DDI fact triplets can be naturally represented as a graph, where each node is a drug and each edge is an interaction between two drugs. Given DDI fact triplets, many graph learning methods have been developed to find unknown interactions between drug-pairs. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have also been applied to the DDI prediction problem, since they can get expressive node embeddings by learning end-to-end from the topological structure and the node features. But known DDI fact triplets are rare, because experiments cost a lot and new drugs keep emerging. For example, the latest DrugBank database has 14,931 drug entries but only 365,984 known DDI fact triplets, which is less than 1% of all potential DDIs. Because of this, over-parameterized deep learning models cannot make full use of their expressive ability and can even perform worse than traditional two-stage embedding methods.

- External KGs and KG-based methods
  - agencies (National Center for Biotechnology Information, European Bioinformatics Institute) maintain public biomedical data resources
  - integrated into KGs: Hetionet, PharmKG, PrimeKG
  - rich prior knowledge, may compensate for lack of samples

  - later works: merge DDI network + KG, extract enclosing subgraphs per drug-pair, predict from concatenated drug node embeddings + subgraph embedding
  - problem: KGs built by automated process or experts -> noise/inconsistent info not filtered
  - leveraging external KGs still challenging
- KnowDDI
  - merge DDI graph + external KG into combined network; learn generic representations for all nodes
  - extract drug-flow subgraph per drug-pair
  - learn knowledge subgraph from generic representations + drug-flow subgraph
  - drug representations become more predictive of DDI types
  - knowledge subgraph has explaining paths: edges of important known DDIs or new edges linking highly similar drugs
  - filters irrelevant info, adds resembling relationships; lack of DDIs compensated by enriched representations + propagated similarities

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Predicting drug-drug interaction (DDI) accurately is important in biomedicine and healthcare. One reason is combination therapies, where several drugs are used together, which can treat complex disease and comorbidities, for example human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). A recent study shows that combination therapies like lopinavir together with ritonavir may also treat coronavirus disease (COVID-19), which is the infectious disease that caused a global pandemic in the past three years. The other reason is that DDI is an important cause of adverse drug reactions. These account for 1% hospitalizations in the general population and 2-5% hospital admissions in the elderly. For example if warfarin and aspirin are taken together, they compete for binding to plasma proteins. The warfarin that cannot be bound to plasma proteins then remains in the blood, and this results in acute bleeding in patients.

Finding DDIs from clinical evidence such as laboratory studies is extremely costly and takes a lot of time. So in recent years computational techniques, especially deep learning, have been developed to speed up finding potential DDIs. DDI fact triplets can be naturally represented as a graph, where each node is a drug and each edge is an interaction between two drugs. Given DDI fact triplets, many graph learning methods have been developed to find unknown interactions between drug-pairs. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have also been applied to the DDI prediction problem, since they can get expressive node embeddings by learning end-to-end from the topological structure and the node features. But known DDI fact triplets are rare, because experiments cost a lot and new drugs keep emerging. For example, the latest DrugBank database has 14,931 drug entries but only 365,984 known DDI fact triplets, which is less than 1% of all potential DDIs. Because of this, over-parameterized deep learning models cannot make full use of their expressive ability and can even perform worse than traditional two-stage embedding methods.

In biomedicine and healthcare, many international agencies such as National Center for Biotechnology Information and European Bioinformatics Institute regularly maintain rich biomedical data resources that are publicly available. Researchers integrate these different and heterogeneous resources into knowledge graphs (KGs) so the information can be used in an organized way. Examples are Hetionet, PharmKG and PrimeKG. These KGs have rich prior knowledge from biomedicine and healthcare, and using them properly may make up for the lack of samples for DDI prediction. The first work to do this was KGNN, which uses external KGs to give topological information for each drug in the target drug-pair. It uniformly samples a fixed size set of neighbors around each drug, and then aggregates the drug features and messages from these neighbors into the drug representation, without considering which drug it interacts with. Later works merge the DDI network with the external KGs into one combined network, extract enclosing subgraphs for different drug-pairs to encode drug-pair specific information, and then predict the DDI for the target drug-pair using the node embeddings of the drugs concatenated with the subgraph embedding. However, these KGs integrate diverse data resources by automated process or by experts, and existing methods cannot filter out noise or inconsistent information. So properly leveraging external KGs is still a challenging problem.

In this paper, we propose KnowDDI, which is an accurate and interpretable method for DDI prediction. First we merge the given DDI graph and an external KG into a combined network, and learn generic representations for all nodes on it to encode generic knowledge. Next we extract a drug-flow subgraph from the combined network for each drug-pair. Then we learn a knowledge subgraph from the generic representations and the drug-flow subgraph. After optimization, the drug representations are transformed so they are more predictive of the DDI types between the target drug-pair. Also, the knowledge subgraph that is returned contains explaining paths which interpret the prediction for the drug-pair. These explaining paths consist only of edges of important known DDIs or of newly-added edges that connect highly similar drugs. So the learned knowledge subgraph filters out irrelevant information and adds resembling relationships between drugs whose interactions are not known. This way the lack of DDIs is implicitly compensated by the enriched drug representations and the propagated drug similarities. We do extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and KnowDDI consistently outperforms existing works. We also do a series of case studies, which show that KnowDDI can find convincing explaining paths that help interpret the DDI prediction results. KnowDDI could be used in a broad range of related interaction prediction tasks, such as protein-protein interactions, drug-target interactions and disease-gene interactions, to help detect potential interactions and in the end advance the development of biomedicine and healthcare.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Accurately predicting drug-drug interaction (DDI) can play an important role in biomedicine and healthcare. On the one hand, combination therapies, where multiple drugs are used together, can be used to treat complex disease and comorbidities, such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) [1,2]. A recent study also shows that combination therapies, such as a combination of lopinavir and ritonavir, may treat coronavirus disease (COVID-19) [3,4,5], the infectious disease which caused a global pandemic in the past three years. On the other hand, DDI is an important cause of adverse drug reactions, which account for 1% hospitalizations in the general population and 2-5% hospital admissions in the elderly [6,7,8]. As a concrete example, if warfarin and aspirin enter the body together, they compete for binding to plasma proteins. The warfarin that cannot be bound to plasma proteins then remains in the blood, which results in acute bleeding in patients [9].

Identifying DDIs by clinical evidence such as laboratory studies is extremely costly and time-consuming [6,8]. In recent years, computational techniques, especially deep learning approaches, have been developed to speed up the discovery of potential DDIs. Naturally, DDI fact triplets can be represented as a graph where each node corresponds to a drug and each edge represents an interaction between two drugs. Given DDI fact triplets, a number of graph learning methods have been developed to identify unknown interactions between drug-pairs. Graph neural networks (GNNs) [10,11], which obtain expressive node embeddings by end-to-end learning from the topological structure and associated node features, have also been applied to the DDI prediction problem. However, known DDI fact triplets are rare due to the high experimental cost and continually emerging new drugs [12]. For example, the latest DrugBank database with 14,931 drug entries only contains 365,984 known DDI fact triplets [13], less than 1% of the total potential DDIs. This prevents over-parameterized deep learning models from using their expressive ability, and they may perform even worse than traditional two-stage embedding methods [14,15].

In biomedicine and healthcare, many international agencies such as National Center for Biotechnology Information and European Bioinformatics Institute regularly maintain rich publicly available biomedical data resources [16]. Researchers then integrate these disparate and heterogeneous resources into knowledge graphs (KGs) to facilitate an organized use of information, for example Hetionet [17,18], PharmKG [19] and PrimeKG [20]. These KGs contain rich prior knowledge discovered in biomedicine and healthcare, and a proper usage of them may compensate for the lack of samples for DDI prediction. The pioneer work KGNN [21] first leverages external KGs to provide topological information for each drug in the target drug-pair. In particular, it uniformly samples a fixed size set of neighbors around each drug, then aggregates drug features and messages from the sampled neighbors into the drug representation without considering which drug it interacts with. Later works merge the DDI network with external KGs into a combined network, extract enclosing subgraphs for different drug-pairs to encode drug-pair specific information, and then predict the DDI for the target drug-pair using the concatenation of the drugs' node embeddings and the embedding of the enclosing subgraph [22,23,24]. However, as these KGs integrate diverse data resources by automated process or experts, existing methods fail to filter out noise or inconsistent information. As a result, properly leveraging external KGs is still a challenging problem.

In this paper, we propose KnowDDI, an accurate and interpretable method for DDI prediction. First, we merge the provided DDI graph and an external KG into a combined network, on which generic representations for all nodes are learned to encode generic knowledge. Next, we extract a drug-flow subgraph for each drug-pair from the combined network. We then learn a knowledge subgraph from the generic representations and the drug-flow subgraph. After optimization, the drug representations are transformed to be more predictive of the DDI types between the target drug-pair. In addition, the returned knowledge subgraph contains explaining paths that interpret the prediction result for the drug-pair; these paths consist only of edges of important known DDIs or newly-added edges connecting highly similar drugs. In other words, the learned knowledge subgraph filters out irrelevant information and adds resembling relationships between drugs whose interactions are unknown. This allows the lack of DDIs to be implicitly compensated by the enriched drug representations and propagated drug similarities. We perform extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and observe that KnowDDI consistently outperforms existing works. A series of case studies further shows that KnowDDI can discover convincing explaining paths which help interpret the DDI prediction results. KnowDDI has the potential to be used in a broad range of related interaction prediction tasks, such as protein-protein interactions, drug-target interactions and disease-gene interactions, to help detect potential interactions and eventually advance the development of biomedicine and healthcare.
